title: Why accuracy lies on imbalanced data
story:
Take a problem where one case in a thousand is positive — fraud, a rare disease, a machine about to fail. Write a model that returns negative for every input. It requires no data, no features and no training, and it is correct 99.9% of the time. Report that number and it sounds like an achievement. The model has not learned anything and will never catch a single case of the thing it was built for.

That is the whole lesson, and it is not a curiosity. It is the default situation in most problems worth building a classifier for, because the interesting events are usually rare. Any measure that does not condition on the rarity of the positive class will reward a model for the prevalence of the negative one, which is a property of the world rather than of the model.

The repair is to use measures whose denominators are the things that are scarce. Of the cases you flagged, how many were real. Of the real cases, how many did you flag. Both are computed from counts that stay small when positives are rare, so neither can be inflated by the size of the negative class. Report them as a pair, and report the base rate beside them, because without the base rate a reader cannot tell a good score from an inevitable one.

The subtler version of this trap catches people who have already learned to avoid the obvious one. Saito and Rehmsmeier examined it in 2015, noting that many studies evaluate classifiers on strongly imbalanced datasets where negatives significantly outweigh positives, and showing that the visual interpretability of the receiver operating characteristic plot on such data can be deceptive with respect to conclusions about the reliability of classification performance — owing, in their diagnosis, to an intuitive but wrong interpretation of specificity. The mechanism is worth seeing. Specificity divides by the number of true negatives, and when negatives are overwhelming that denominator is enormous, so a large absolute number of false alarms still produces a specificity close to one and a curve that hugs the corner. The plot looks excellent while the queue of flagged cases is mostly noise.

Their alternative addresses it directly, because precision evaluates the fraction of true positives among positive predictions — a quantity that depends on prevalence, which is exactly why it does not flatter a classifier on skewed data. And the relationship between the two spaces is exact but narrower than it is usually taken to be: a curve dominates in one if and only if it dominates in the other, while the areas are not interchangeable and an algorithm optimising one is not guaranteed to optimise the other.

problem.name: Base rate dependence
problem.shape: One class is far rarer than the other, and the measure being used rewards getting the common class right.
tell: the positive class is a small percentage of the data
a headline score is very high and nobody has stated the base rate
a receiver operating characteristic curve looks excellent and the flagged queue is mostly noise
no trivial baseline has been computed for comparison
problem.move: State the base rate alongside every score, and compute what the majority-class rule would achieve before reporting anything. Use measures whose denominators are the scarce quantities — the flagged cases and the real cases — and prefer the precision-recall view when the classes are strongly skewed.
problem.invariant: A measure that does not condition on the rarity of the positive class rewards the prevalence of the negative one. Prevalence is a property of the world, not of the model.
problem.breaks: Measures that condition on prevalence inherit it, so they do not transfer between populations. A precision figure obtained where positives are one in a thousand does not describe performance where they are one in fifty, even with the identical model and the identical threshold.

cost.time: none; the base rate and the trivial baseline are both arithmetic
cost.beats: a single proportion of correct answers, which on skewed data measures the skew, and specificity-based summaries, which hide large absolute numbers of false alarms behind an enormous denominator

worked.problem: Your model is 99.9% accurate on a rare-event problem. What does that tell you?
worked.reasoning:
On its own, almost nothing — and the first thing to establish is what the number would have been without a model at all.

If one case in a thousand is positive, the rule that always answers negative scores 99.9% without any data, features or fitting. So the headline figure is exactly what a constant function achieves, and the useful quantity was never the accuracy but the distance between it and that floor. Quoted without the base rate, the number is uninterpretable rather than impressive.

The mechanism is that accuracy does not condition on the rarity of the positive class, so it is dominated by performance on the negative one, and the prevalence of negatives is a fact about the world rather than about the model. Any measure with that property will reward you for the problem's skew.

So I would ask for the four counts, and compute precision and recall. Both divide by quantities that stay small when positives are rare — what you flagged, and what was really there — so neither can be inflated by the size of the negative class. And I would report them as a pair with the base rate stated alongside, because a reader cannot otherwise distinguish a good score from an inevitable one.

The version of this that catches more experienced people is the receiver operating characteristic curve, which feels like the sophisticated answer and is not safe here. Specificity divides by the number of true negatives, and when negatives overwhelm the data that denominator is enormous, so a large absolute number of false alarms still yields a specificity near one and a curve hugging the corner. The plot looks excellent while the flagged queue is mostly noise. That is the documented finding: on strongly imbalanced data the visual interpretability of such plots can be deceptive with respect to conclusions about reliability, owing to an intuitive but wrong interpretation of specificity. Precision does not have this failure because it evaluates the fraction of true positives among positive predictions, and so depends on prevalence.

One technical caution I would add. The two curve spaces are related exactly — dominance in one implies dominance in the other — but the areas are not interchangeable, and an algorithm optimising one is not guaranteed to optimise the other. So the equivalence does not license swapping the summaries.

And the constructive answer, rather than only the critique: decide what the flagged cases cost and what the missed ones cost, and evaluate against that. On rare-event problems the honest measure is usually expected cost, and the honest comparison is always against the trivial rule.

problem.practice: Compute the accuracy of the always-negative rule on your data and write it next to your model's accuracy. Then produce precision and recall for both. Finally, if you use a receiver operating characteristic curve, count the absolute number of false alarms at your operating point and check whether that queue is workable.

beats.broke: When almost every case is negative, a rule that never predicts the positive class is correct almost every time — so the proportion of correct answers is high and the classifier is useless.
beats.fix: Report measures that condition on the rare thing — what fraction of flagged cases were real, and what fraction of real cases were flagged — and always state the base rate beside any score.
beats.cost: Measures that condition on prevalence move when prevalence moves, so a score obtained on one population does not transfer to another with a different mix.

interview.q: Your model is 99.9% accurate on a rare-event problem. What does that tell you?
interview.trap: Switching to a receiver operating characteristic curve and considering the problem solved. Specificity divides by an enormous number of true negatives, so a large absolute number of false alarms still produces a curve that hugs the corner while the flagged queue is mostly noise.
interview.answer:

THE ONE-LINE DEMONSTRATION

   1 in 1000 positive
   "return negative, always"
      -> 99.9% accurate
      -> catches nothing, ever

   your headline number was the FLOOR.

WHY

   accuracy does not condition on rarity
   -> dominated by the NEGATIVE class
   -> prevalence is a fact about THE WORLD

USE SCARCE DENOMINATORS

   PRECISION  / flagged
   RECALL     / really there

   report AS A PAIR + THE BASE RATE.

THE SECOND TRAP

   specificity = TN / (TN + FP)
   negatives overwhelming -> TN enormous
   -> many false alarms, specificity still ~1
   -> curve hugs the corner
   -> the plot looks excellent, the queue is noise

   "an intuitive but wrong interpretation of
    specificity"

   precision DEPENDS on prevalence --
   which is precisely why it does not flatter.

THE LIMIT OF THE EQUIVALENCE

   dominance transfers between the two spaces.
   AREA DOES NOT.

THE CARRY-OVER COST

   prevalence-dependent measures do not TRANSFER.
   precision at 1-in-1000 does not describe
   1-in-50, same model, same threshold.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD

   cost of a flagged case?
   cost of a missed one?
   -> expected cost, against the trivial rule.
takeaway: Any measure that does not condition on the rare class rewards you for how common the other one is — which is why the always-negative rule scores 99.9% and why a curve built on specificity can hug the corner while the flagged queue is mostly noise.
